Introduction

Purpose of this Document

The Enterprise Architecture Autonomous Enterprise Governance & Operating Model establishes the canonical methodology for governing, controlling, engineering, operating, assuring, and continuously evolving Autonomous Enterprise capabilities within the MFM Enterprise Architecture Framework.

An Autonomous Enterprise is an enterprise capable of intelligently coordinating human expertise, business capabilities, digital platforms, Artificial Intelligence (AI), Agentic AI, autonomous services, intelligent workflows, enterprise information, governance mechanisms, cybersecurity, resilience, and continuous learning into a continuously adaptive operating model.

Unlike conventional digital enterprises that primarily automate predefined activities, Autonomous Enterprises increasingly observe, understand, reason, predict, decide, execute, monitor, learn, and optimize while maintaining human governance, transparency, accountability, resilience, security, and ethical responsibility.

EA-IMETA76 establishes the governance foundation required to ensure that increasing autonomy does not result in uncontrolled enterprise behavior.

The objective is not unrestricted autonomy.

The objective is:

Maximum useful autonomy within explicitly defined authority, governance, security, risk, accountability, and architectural boundaries.

Governance Objectives

The objectives of EA-IMETA76 are to:

establish Autonomous Enterprise governance principles

define governance structures for autonomous organizations

establish explicit authority and decision rights

define autonomy boundaries

integrate governance into Enterprise Architecture

establish continuous governance and assurance

strengthen autonomous accountability

enable policy-driven autonomous execution

establish governance evidence and traceability

support human–AI governance collaboration

strengthen enterprise resilience

enable continuous governance evolution

maximize Sustainable Enterprise Value

Scope

EA-IMETA76 applies to:

Enterprise Architecture Governance

An Autonomous Enterprise shall operate through a continuous governance cycle:

This adaptive governance cycle establishes the foundation for responsible enterprise autonomy.

Governance is therefore not limited to approval before execution or audit after execution.

Governance becomes an active architectural capability operating continuously throughout the enterprise lifecycle.

1. Enterprise Autonomous Governance Foundation

1.1 Purpose

The Enterprise Autonomous Governance Foundation establishes the canonical governance model for Autonomous Enterprise capabilities operating within the MFM Enterprise Architecture Framework.

The framework defines how autonomous capabilities shall be:

authorized

governed

controlled

monitored

measured

assured

corrected

suspended

recovered

evolved

Enterprise Architects shall ensure autonomous capabilities remain aligned with enterprise strategy, governance policies, risk appetite, regulatory obligations, security requirements, and Sustainable Enterprise Value objectives.

1.2 Autonomous Enterprise Governance Model

The recommended logical governance architecture consists of:

Enterprise Strategy

↓

Executive Governance

↓

Enterprise Architecture Governance

↓

Autonomous Governance

↓

Policy & Authority Layer

↓

Autonomous Capability Layer

↓

Operational Execution

↓

Continuous Observability

↓

Assurance & Compliance

↓

Governance Learning

↓

Architecture Evolution

Each layer shall remain connected to the layers above and below it.

Governance shall therefore operate as an integrated enterprise control system rather than as a collection of isolated governance activities.

1.3 Governance as an Architectural Capability

Governance shall be treated as a formal Enterprise Architecture capability.

The governance capability shall provide the enterprise with the ability to:

establish policies

define authority

define decision rights

establish autonomy boundaries

enforce architectural constraints

monitor autonomous execution

collect governance evidence

detect deviations

manage exceptions

escalate decisions

suspend autonomous capabilities

recover from unacceptable outcomes

continuously improve governance

The architecture must be capable of answering:

WHO IS AUTHORIZED?

WHAT ARE THEY AUTHORIZED TO DO?

WHY ARE THEY AUTHORIZED?

UNDER WHICH POLICY?

WITH WHICH INFORMATION?

USING WHICH SYSTEM?

WITH WHICH LEVEL OF AUTONOMY?

WITH WHICH RISK?

FOR HOW LONG?

UNDER WHICH CONDITIONS?

WHAT HAPPENS IF SOMETHING GOES WRONG?

1.4 Governance Evolution

Traditional enterprise governance can be represented as:

Plan

↓

Review

↓

Approve

↓

Implement

↓

Operate

↓

Audit

Autonomous enterprise governance evolves toward:

↓

↓

↓

↓

Observation

↓

Intervention

↓

Learning

↓

This represents a fundamental transformation from periodic governance toward continuous governance.

The enterprise must increasingly govern autonomous capabilities while they are operating rather than relying exclusively on governance activities performed before or after execution.

1.5 Governance by Design

EA-IMETA76 establishes the principle:

Governance shall be designed into the enterprise architecture rather than added after implementation.

Governance requirements shall therefore be considered during:

strategy development

capability design

process design

information architecture

application architecture

integration architecture

technology architecture

AI architecture

agent architecture

security architecture

operating-model design

Every autonomous capability shall have governance designed into its architecture.

This shall include:

Identity

Authority

Access

Policy

Decision Rights

Boundaries

Observability

Auditability

Escalation

Fail-Safe

Recovery

Termination

Evidence

1.6 Autonomous Authority

Autonomous authority is defined as:

The explicitly delegated ability of an autonomous capability to perform specified decisions or actions within defined enterprise boundaries.

Autonomous authority shall never be assumed.

It shall be:

defined

approved

delegated

constrained

monitored

reviewed

revocable

The authority relationship is:

Enterprise

↓

Governance Authority

↓

Capability Owner

↓

Autonomous Capability

↓

Agent / System

↓

Action

The autonomous capability does not become the source of authority.

It receives authority from the enterprise.

Capability and authority shall therefore remain separate architectural concepts.

1.7 Autonomy Boundary

Every autonomous capability shall operate within an explicitly defined Autonomy Boundary.

The autonomy boundary shall define:

Purpose

What the autonomous capability exists to accomplish.

Authority

Which decisions it is permitted to make.

Data

Which information it may access and process.

Tools

Which systems, services, APIs, and tools it may use.

Actions

Which actions it may execute.

Financial Limit

Which financial consequences it may initiate.

Risk Limit

Which level of risk it may assume.

Temporal Limit

How long its authority remains valid.

Geographic Limit

Where the capability may operate, where applicable.

Escalation Threshold

When human intervention becomes mandatory.

Termination Condition

When autonomous execution must stop.

The resulting governance envelope is:

Autonomous Capability
        |
        +-- Purpose
        +-- Authority
        +-- Data
        +-- Tools
        +-- Actions
        +-- Financial Limit
        +-- Risk Limit
        +-- Temporal Limit
        +-- Geographic Limit
        +-- Escalation Threshold
        +-- Termination Condition

No autonomous capability shall be considered fully production-ready until its autonomy boundary has been defined and approved.

1.8 Governance Decision Rights

EA-IMETA76 establishes four fundamental decision categories.

Category A – Human Decision

The decision must be made directly by an authorized human.

Typical examples include:

strategic direction

enterprise policy

major investment

significant risk acceptance

ethical decisions

major organizational change

Category B – Human-Approved Autonomous Decision

An autonomous capability may prepare, analyze, simulate, or recommend the decision.

Execution requires human approval.

Typical examples include:

major financial commitments

significant contractual commitments

major architecture changes

exceptional risk decisions

Category C – Bounded Autonomous Decision

The autonomous capability may execute the decision without individual human approval because authority has already been delegated.

Typical examples include:

routine workflow decisions

standard service provisioning

resource optimization

predefined operational remediation

Category D – Automated Control Action

The architecture automatically performs an authorized control action when predefined conditions are detected.

Typical examples include:

blocking unauthorized access

isolating a compromised service

restarting a failed service

enforcing security controls

triggering predefined continuity procedures

1.9 Continuous Governance

Traditional governance relies heavily upon periodic checkpoints.

EA-IMETA76 establishes continuous governance as the preferred model for autonomous capabilities.

The continuous governance lifecycle is:

Define

↓

Authorize

↓

Execute

↓

Observe

↓

Evaluate

↓

Correct

↓

Learn

↓

Adapt

Continuous governance requires continuous access to:

operational telemetry

decisions

events

policy evaluations

authorization records

system actions

exceptions

performance data

risk indicators

security events

The enterprise must therefore treat observability as a governance capability.

An autonomous capability that cannot be adequately observed cannot be adequately governed.

1.10 Governance Evidence

EA-IMETA76 establishes Governance Evidence as a formal architectural information domain.

Governance evidence may include:

identity

authority

policy

decision

data source

model

agent

tool

action

timestamp

result

exception

intervention

approval

outcome

The enterprise shall be able to determine:

WHO OR WHAT ACTED?

WHAT WAS DONE?

WHY WAS IT DONE?

WHICH POLICY APPLIED?

WHICH AUTHORITY WAS USED?

WHICH INFORMATION WAS USED?

WHICH MODEL OR AGENT WAS INVOLVED?

WHICH TOOLS WERE USED?

WHAT WAS THE RESULT?

WAS HUMAN INTERVENTION REQUIRED?

WHAT EVIDENCE EXISTS?

Governance evidence shall therefore be treated as an enterprise information asset.

1.11 Governance Feedback Loop

The EA-IMETA76 governance feedback loop is:

Enterprise Intent

↓

Governance Policy

↓

Architectural Constraint

↓

Autonomous Capability

↓

Operational Execution

↓

Telemetry / Evidence

↓

Governance Evaluation

↓

↓

↓

Architecture Evolution

↓

↓

Enterprise Intent

This creates a closed-loop governance architecture.

The enterprise does not merely govern autonomous systems.

It continuously learns from their operation and uses that learning to improve:

policies

controls

architecture

operating models

autonomy boundaries

risk management

governance mechanisms

1.12 Governance and Accountability

Autonomous execution shall not create an accountability gap.

The enterprise shall therefore distinguish between:

Authority

Execution

Accountability

Responsibility

Liability

Assurance

An autonomous system may execute an action.

However, the enterprise must still be able to identify:

who authorized the capability

who owns the capability

who defined its operating boundaries

who is responsible for monitoring it

who receives escalations

who can suspend it

who reviews its performance

Therefore:

Autonomous execution does not eliminate human accountability; it changes how accountability must be architecturally represented.

1.13 Relationship to the MFM Enterprise Architecture

EA-IMETA76 provides the governance and operating-model layer for the autonomous capabilities established throughout the preceding EA-IMETA architecture.

It provides the mechanism through which the enterprise can evolve from:

Designed Enterprise

↓

Managed Digital Enterprise

↓

Intelligent Enterprise

↓

Autonomous Enterprise

while preserving:

strategic alignment

governance

security

accountability

resilience

architectural integrity

operational control

transparency

The objective is therefore not maximum autonomy.

The objective is:

Maximum useful autonomy within minimum acceptable risk and clearly defined enterprise authority.

1.14 Core EA-IMETA76 Governance Principles

EA-IMETA76 establishes the following foundational principles.

Principle 01 – Governance by Design

Governance shall be incorporated into architecture from the beginning.

Principle 02 – Explicit Authority

No autonomous capability shall possess authority that has not been explicitly delegated.

Principle 03 – Bounded Autonomy

Autonomous capabilities shall operate within defined boundaries.

Principle 04 – Continuous Observability

Autonomous execution shall be observable throughout its operational lifecycle.

Principle 05 – Evidence-Based Governance

Governance decisions shall be supported by verifiable evidence.

Principle 06 – Policy Enforcement

Critical policies shall be technically enforceable wherever practical.

Principle 07 – Human Accountability

Human accountability shall remain identifiable even when execution is autonomous.

Principle 08 – Exception Management

Autonomous capabilities shall have defined mechanisms for handling exceptions.

Principle 09 – Reversibility

Autonomous actions shall be reversible, containable, or otherwise recoverable where technically and operationally feasible.

Principle 10 – Revocable Authority

Autonomous authority shall be capable of being suspended or revoked.

Principle 11 – Risk-Proportional Autonomy

The degree of autonomy shall correspond to the risk and consequence of the activity.

Principle 12 – Continuous Evolution

Governance shall continuously evolve as the enterprise, technology, risks, regulations, and autonomous capabilities change.

Implementation Characteristics

The Enterprise Autonomous Governance Foundation shall remain:

purpose-driven

governance-controlled

policy-based

human-accountable

autonomy-enabled

observable

measurable

resilient

explainable

strategically aligned

continuously evolving

These implementation characteristics establish the governance foundation for the Autonomous Enterprise, enabling Enterprise Architects to design organizations in which autonomous capabilities can operate with clearly delegated authority, continuous observability, transparent accountability, controlled risk, and measurable Sustainable Enterprise Value.

Conclusion

EA-IMETA76 establishes the conceptual foundation for the Enterprise Architecture Autonomous Enterprise Governance & Operating Model.

The central architectural transformation is:

Governance as Periodic Control → Governance as Continuous Enterprise Capability

The Autonomous Enterprise must therefore connect:

Human Intent → Policy → Authority → Autonomy → Execution → Evidence → Assurance → Learning → Evolution

The fundamental EA-IMETA76 principle is:

Autonomy shall never exist outside governance. Governance shall never exist without the ability to observe and control execution.

This governance foundation will support the subsequent EA-IMETA76 sections covering the autonomous enterprise operating model, governance structures, authority models, policy engineering, continuous assurance, autonomous risk management, governance intelligence, and enterprise evolution.

1. Enterprise Autonomous Operating Model Framework

1.1 Purpose

The Enterprise Autonomous Operating Model Framework establishes the canonical methodology for designing, governing, engineering, integrating, operating, measuring, and continuously evolving enterprise operating models capable of autonomous execution within defined governance boundaries.

An Autonomous Operating Model coordinates enterprise strategy, governance, business capabilities, organizational structures, intelligent agents, Artificial Intelligence, enterprise information, applications, technology platforms, human expertise, operational processes, and autonomous decision-making into one adaptive enterprise operating system.

Unlike traditional operating models that primarily define how people, processes, and technology perform predefined activities, an Autonomous Operating Model continuously coordinates human and machine capabilities according to enterprise policies, delegated authority, operational conditions, risk requirements, and measurable enterprise outcomes.

Enterprise Architects shall ensure that autonomy enhances enterprise performance while preserving executive accountability, governance integrity, regulatory compliance, operational resilience, human oversight, and Sustainable Enterprise Value.

1.2 Objectives

The Enterprise Autonomous Operating Model Framework shall:

establish enterprise-wide autonomous operating model principles

define autonomous operating structures

strengthen strategic alignment

integrate human and machine capabilities

enable policy-driven autonomous execution

improve operational adaptability

strengthen governance integration

improve enterprise resilience

support continuous optimization

preserve executive accountability

maximize Sustainable Enterprise Value

Enterprise strategy, mission alignment, strategic priorities, transformation governance, investment direction, enterprise capabilities, and long-term organizational evolution.

Business Operating Model

Organizational Operating Model

Information Operating Model

Enterprise information management, knowledge management, semantic interoperability, information ownership, data stewardship, enterprise memory, knowledge graphs, and Digital Twin synchronization.

Technology Operating Model

Applications, APIs, platforms, cloud services, infrastructure, AI platforms, agent platforms, integration services, observability platforms, and technology lifecycle management.

Autonomous Operations Model

Autonomous workflows, intelligent orchestration, agent collaboration, AI-assisted decision-making, autonomous execution, event-driven operations, adaptive optimization, and exception management.

Governance Operating Model

Architecture governance, policy management, delegated authority, decision rights, compliance, risk management, security governance, executive oversight, and continuous assurance.

Sustainability Operating Model

Responsible automation, environmental stewardship, ESG management, resource optimization, sustainable technology, responsible innovation, and long-term enterprise sustainability.

2.7 Governance Control Model

Governance controls shall operate across five control modes.

Preventive Controls

Controls designed to prevent unauthorized or unsafe actions before execution.

Detective Controls

Controls designed to identify deviations, anomalies, policy violations, or unexpected behavior.

Corrective Controls

Controls designed to restore the enterprise to an approved operating condition.

Compensating Controls

Controls designed to reduce risk where primary controls cannot fully prevent an undesired condition.

Adaptive Controls

Controls capable of evolving in response to validated changes in risk, policy, technology, operating conditions, or enterprise requirements.

The governance control model is therefore:

Prevent

↓

Detect

↓

Correct

↓

Compensate

↓

Adapt

3. Enterprise Autonomous Decision Governance Framework

3.1 Purpose

The Enterprise Autonomous Decision Governance Framework establishes the canonical methodology for governing enterprise decisions that are increasingly supported, augmented, recommended, or executed by Artificial Intelligence, intelligent agents, autonomous services, decision engines, and automated enterprise capabilities.

The framework establishes the relationship between enterprise intent, decision authority, decision context, intelligence, policy, risk, human oversight, autonomous execution, evidence, and continuous learning.

Enterprise Architects shall ensure that autonomous decision-making remains aligned with enterprise strategy, governance policies, architectural principles, regulatory requirements, risk appetite, operational objectives, and Sustainable Enterprise Value.

Autonomous decision-making shall therefore augment enterprise intelligence without creating uncontrolled or unaccountable decision authority.

3.2 Objectives

The Enterprise Autonomous Decision Governance Framework shall:

establish enterprise-wide decision governance principles

define autonomous decision boundaries

establish decision authority

strengthen decision transparency

support human–AI decision collaboration

improve decision quality

strengthen decision traceability

integrate risk into autonomous decisions

enable policy-driven decision execution

strengthen executive decision confidence

support continuous decision learning

maximize Sustainable Enterprise Value

3.3 Autonomous Decision Architecture

The recommended logical architecture consists of:

Enterprise Intent

↓

Strategic Objectives

↓

Governance Policy

↓

Decision Authority

↓

Decision Context

↓

Enterprise Intelligence

↓

AI / Agent Analysis

↓

Decision Recommendation

↓

Human or Autonomous Decision

↓

Governed Execution

↓

Outcome

↓

Evidence

↓

Decision Evaluation

↓

Continuous Learning

Each decision layer shall remain governed by enterprise policies, authority boundaries, risk controls, and measurable decision objectives.

3.4 Decision Governance Domains

Enterprise Autonomous Decision Governance shall govern:

Strategic Decisions

Enterprise strategy, organizational direction, investment priorities, transformation decisions, strategic partnerships, enterprise architecture direction, and long-term capability development.

Tactical Decisions

Portfolio decisions, resource allocation, program priorities, capability investments, operational optimization, workforce planning, and technology decisions.

Operational Decisions

Workflow execution, service orchestration, resource optimization, incident response, customer interaction, operational scheduling, and routine enterprise decisions.

Autonomous Control Decisions

Predefined automated decisions that protect enterprise operations, security, resilience, compliance, or continuity.

Examples include:

access blocking

service isolation

automated remediation

capacity adjustment

workflow routing

security response

continuity activation

Exceptional Decisions

Decisions outside predefined authority, policy, risk, or operational boundaries.

Exceptional decisions shall be escalated to an authorized human or governance authority.

3.5 Decision Authority Model

Decision authority shall be explicitly defined for every material autonomous decision capability.

Authority shall specify:

decision owner

decision authority

decision scope

permitted actions

information access

financial limits

risk limits

escalation conditions

human approval requirements

review frequency

suspension conditions

The authority relationship is:

Enterprise Authority

↓

Governance Authority

↓

Decision Owner

↓

Decision Capability

↓

AI / Agent

↓

Decision

↓

Action

Autonomous decision capability shall never be interpreted as autonomous authority.

The capability may analyze or execute only within authority delegated by the enterprise.

3.6 Decision Autonomy Levels

EA-IMETA76 establishes a graduated autonomy model.

Level 0 – Human Only

The decision is performed entirely by a human.

AI and automation may provide information but shall not make or execute the decision.

Level 1 – AI Assisted

AI provides information, analysis, classification, prediction, or recommendations.

The human makes and executes the decision.

Level 2 – AI Recommended

AI or an intelligent agent generates a formal decision recommendation.

A human reviews and approves the recommendation before execution.

Level 3 – Human-Supervised Autonomous

The autonomous capability may make and execute predefined decisions within an approved authority boundary.

Human oversight remains active through monitoring and exception management.

Level 4 – Bounded Autonomous

The autonomous capability may independently analyze, decide, execute, monitor, and optimize predefined activities within approved policy, risk, and authority boundaries.

Human intervention is triggered by defined escalation conditions.

Level 5 – Adaptive Autonomous

The autonomous capability may continuously adapt decision behavior within approved governance constraints based on operational evidence, validated learning, changing context, and defined performance objectives.

Material changes to authority, risk boundaries, or enterprise policy remain subject to governance approval.

3.7 Decision Context

Autonomous decisions shall be made within a defined decision context.

Decision context may include:

enterprise objectives

business conditions

operational state

customer context

financial context

risk context

security context

regulatory context

environmental context

historical information

current telemetry

relevant policies

applicable authority

Decision context shall remain traceable to the information and conditions that influenced the decision.

3.8 Policy-Driven Decision Governance

Autonomous decision capabilities shall operate according to explicit enterprise policies.

Policies shall define:

permitted behavior

prohibited behavior

authority boundaries

risk thresholds

escalation thresholds

decision constraints

information requirements

execution requirements

monitoring requirements

termination conditions

Where technically feasible, critical policies shall be represented as machine-readable controls capable of being evaluated during autonomous decision execution.

This establishes the relationship:

Policy

↓

Decision Constraint

↓

Decision Evaluation

↓

Authorized Decision

↓

Controlled Action

3.9 Decision Risk Governance

Every autonomous decision capability shall be assessed according to:

decision impact

financial consequence

operational consequence

security consequence

regulatory consequence

reputational consequence

reversibility

uncertainty

dependency

potential cascading effect

Decision autonomy shall therefore be proportional to decision risk.

High-impact and difficult-to-reverse decisions shall require stronger governance and greater human involvement.

Low-risk, repeatable, reversible decisions may be delegated to higher levels of autonomy where appropriate controls exist.

3.10 Human Oversight

Human oversight shall remain available according to decision risk and autonomy level.

Human oversight mechanisms may include:

approval

review

monitoring

exception handling

override

suspension

escalation

post-decision assessment

periodic governance review

The objective is not to require humans to manually approve every autonomous decision.

The objective is to ensure that humans remain capable of exercising meaningful authority over decisions that exceed autonomous boundaries.

3.11 Decision Evidence

Material autonomous decisions shall generate appropriate evidence.

Decision evidence may include:

decision identity

decision timestamp

decision owner

autonomous capability identity

applicable policy

authority used

decision context

information sources

AI model

agent

recommendation

decision

action

outcome

exception

human intervention

Decision evidence shall support:

auditability

explainability

accountability

incident investigation

compliance

performance management

governance improvement

enterprise learning

3.12 Decision Explainability

Autonomous decision capabilities shall provide an appropriate level of explainability according to decision significance.

Explainability shall enable the enterprise to understand:

what decision was made

why the decision was made

which information influenced the decision

which policy applied

which authority was used

which model or agent participated

what action followed

what outcome resulted

The level of explanation shall be proportional to:

decision impact

risk

regulatory requirements

stakeholder requirements

reversibility

3.13 Decision Exception Management

Autonomous decision capabilities shall identify and manage conditions outside their approved operating boundaries.

Exceptions may include:

insufficient information

conflicting policies

insufficient authority

excessive risk

unexpected system behavior

anomalous conditions

model uncertainty

security events

regulatory constraints

unavailable dependencies

The exception lifecycle shall be:

Exception Detection

↓

Classification

↓

Risk Assessment

↓

Escalation

↓

Human / Governance Decision

↓

Controlled Resolution

↓

Evidence

↓

Learning

Exceptions shall become inputs to governance improvement and autonomous capability evolution.

3.14 Decision Override

The enterprise shall maintain the ability to override autonomous decisions where required.

Override mechanisms may include:

human intervention

governance intervention

policy change

authority revocation

capability suspension

service isolation

emergency shutdown

Override mechanisms shall be tested periodically to ensure they remain operationally effective.

3.15 Decision Monitoring

Decision governance shall continuously monitor:

decision volume

decision quality

decision accuracy

exception rates

override rates

escalation rates

policy violations

decision latency

outcome quality

financial impact

operational impact

risk exposure

Decision monitoring shall support both operational control and long-term governance improvement.

3.16 Decision Learning

The enterprise shall use decision outcomes to improve:

decision policies

decision models

authority boundaries

escalation thresholds

operating procedures

autonomous capabilities

governance controls

enterprise architecture

The learning cycle is:

Decision

↓

Outcome

↓

Evaluation

↓

Feedback

↓

Learning

↓

Governance Improvement

↓

Architecture Evolution

Learning shall remain governed.

Autonomous learning shall not independently create new enterprise authority without appropriate governance approval.

4. Enterprise Human–AI Governance Collaboration Framework

4.1 Purpose

The Enterprise Human–AI Governance Collaboration Framework establishes the canonical methodology for coordinating human expertise, Artificial Intelligence, intelligent agents, autonomous services, and enterprise governance mechanisms.

The framework defines how humans and intelligent systems shall collaborate in strategic, tactical, operational, analytical, and governance activities while maintaining clear accountability, authority, transparency, security, and enterprise control.

The objective is not to replace human governance with machine governance.

The objective is to create a governance system in which human judgment and machine intelligence reinforce one another.

4.2 Objectives

The Enterprise Human–AI Governance Collaboration Framework shall:

define human–AI governance roles

establish collaboration principles

clarify human and machine responsibilities

strengthen decision quality

improve governance responsiveness

preserve human accountability

enable intelligent governance support

strengthen explainability

improve enterprise resilience

support responsible autonomy

maximize Sustainable Enterprise Value

4.3 Human–AI Governance Model

The recommended logical model consists of:

Human Governance

↓

Enterprise Intent

↓

Governance Policy

↓

AI / Agent Intelligence

↓

Decision Support

↓

Human Judgment

↓

Governed Decision

↓

Autonomous or Human Execution

↓

Observation

↓

Evidence

↓

Human–AI Learning

Human governance remains the source of enterprise purpose, authority, accountability, and policy.

AI and autonomous systems provide intelligence, analysis, prediction, orchestration, and bounded execution.

4.4 Human Governance Responsibilities

Humans shall remain responsible for:

enterprise purpose

strategic direction

governance principles

risk appetite

ethical boundaries

major investment decisions

organizational accountability

authority delegation

policy approval

exceptional decisions

governance intervention

Humans shall also retain the ability to:

question autonomous decisions

override autonomous actions

suspend capabilities

revoke authority

change policies

initiate governance review

4.5 AI Governance Responsibilities

AI systems and intelligent agents may support:

information analysis

pattern recognition

forecasting

scenario analysis

risk detection

decision recommendation

policy evaluation

operational optimization

anomaly detection

governance monitoring

evidence generation

AI systems shall not independently assume enterprise authority outside explicitly delegated boundaries.

4.6 Human–AI Decision Collaboration

Human–AI collaboration shall support multiple operating modes.

Human-Led

The human makes the decision and AI provides supporting information.

AI-Assisted

AI performs analysis and recommendation while the human remains the decision-maker.

AI-Recommended

AI produces a formal recommendation requiring human approval.

Human-Supervised Autonomous

The AI or agent makes bounded decisions while humans supervise performance and exceptions.

Bounded Autonomous

The AI or agent independently executes approved decisions within predefined authority and risk boundaries.

Adaptive Autonomous

The AI or agent continuously optimizes approved activities while remaining constrained by enterprise policy and governance.

4.7 Trust Model

Human trust in autonomous systems shall be based on evidence rather than assumption.

Trust shall be supported by:

transparency

explainability

performance evidence

policy compliance

security assurance

reliability

resilience

auditability

predictable behavior

effective override mechanisms

Trust shall therefore be continuously evaluated.

The enterprise shall not assume that historical performance automatically guarantees future trustworthiness.

4.8 Human–AI Escalation

AI and autonomous systems shall escalate when:

authority is insufficient

risk exceeds approved thresholds

policy conflicts exist

information is insufficient

uncertainty is excessive

system dependencies fail

security conditions change materially

unexpected behavior is detected

ethical considerations arise

decision consequences exceed approved limits

Escalation shall transfer the decision to an appropriately authorized human or governance authority.

4.9 Human–AI Accountability

Human–AI collaboration shall maintain explicit accountability.

The enterprise shall identify:

human owner

capability owner

system owner

agent owner

governance owner

operational owner

decision authority

escalation authority

Accountability shall remain visible even when execution is fully automated.

4.10 Human–AI Governance Learning

The enterprise shall continuously evaluate how effectively humans and AI collaborate.

Evaluation shall consider:

decision quality

human intervention

override frequency

escalation quality

trust

productivity

operational resilience

governance effectiveness

stakeholder outcomes

The results shall inform:

operating model evolution

governance improvement

workforce development

AI capability development

agent capability development

architecture evolution

4.11 Implementation Characteristics

The Enterprise Autonomous Decision Governance Framework and the Enterprise Human–AI Governance Collaboration Framework shall remain:

purpose-driven

governance-controlled

policy-based

human-accountable

risk-proportional

explainable

observable

measurable

resilient

interoperable

strategically aligned

continuously evolving

These implementation characteristics establish the decision and human–AI governance foundation of the Autonomous Enterprise, enabling Enterprise Architects to engineer organizations in which intelligent systems can support and execute governed decisions while humans retain meaningful authority, accountability, oversight, and the ability to intervene.

5. Enterprise Autonomous Policy Engineering Framework

5.1 Purpose

The Enterprise Autonomous Policy Engineering Framework establishes the canonical methodology for designing, expressing, implementing, enforcing, monitoring, evaluating, and continuously evolving enterprise policies within an Autonomous Enterprise.

Traditional enterprise policies are frequently expressed as documents intended primarily for human interpretation.

Autonomous enterprises require policies that can also be interpreted and enforced by digital systems, Artificial Intelligence, intelligent agents, automated workflows, governance engines, and operational platforms.

Enterprise Architects shall therefore ensure that policies remain understandable to humans while becoming sufficiently structured, traceable, testable, enforceable, and measurable for autonomous execution.

The objective is not to replace human policy authority with machine policy authority.

The objective is to transform approved enterprise intent into enforceable architectural controls.

5.2 Objectives

The Enterprise Autonomous Policy Engineering Framework shall:

establish enterprise-wide autonomous policy engineering standards

improve policy consistency

strengthen policy traceability

enable machine-readable policy

improve policy enforcement

strengthen governance automation

improve policy testing

reduce policy ambiguity

strengthen regulatory alignment

enable continuous policy evolution

maximize Sustainable Enterprise Value

5.3 Autonomous Policy Architecture

The recommended logical architecture consists of:

Enterprise Intent

↓

Governance Principle

↓

Enterprise Policy

↓

Policy Rule

↓

Machine-Readable Policy

↓

Policy Evaluation

↓

Runtime Enforcement

↓

Governance Evidence

↓

Policy Performance

↓

Policy Evolution

Policies shall remain connected to the enterprise objectives, authorities, capabilities, risks, controls, and outcomes they govern.

5.4 Policy Domains

Enterprise Autonomous Policy Engineering shall govern:

Strategic Policies

Enterprise strategy, enterprise principles, strategic priorities, investment direction, organizational policy, and long-term enterprise development.

Business Policies

Business rules, customer policies, service policies, financial policies, procurement policies, operational policies, and process requirements.

Information Policies

Data ownership, information classification, data quality, information access, retention, provenance, privacy, knowledge management, and information lifecycle requirements.

Technology Policies

Approved technologies, platform standards, architecture standards, integration requirements, cloud policies, application standards, and technology lifecycle requirements.

AI Policies

Artificial Intelligence usage, model governance, responsible AI, explainability, model risk, AI lifecycle requirements, training data requirements, and AI assurance.

Agent Policies

Agent identity, delegated authority, tool access, decision boundaries, interaction rules, agent collaboration, escalation, and agent lifecycle requirements.

Security Policies

Identity, Zero Trust, access control, cybersecurity, threat response, encryption, security monitoring, resilience, and incident requirements.

Governance Policies

Decision rights, Architecture Decision Records (ADRs), compliance, audit, risk governance, exception management, authority delegation, and executive oversight.

5.5 Policy Lifecycle

Enterprise autonomous policies shall progress through:

↓

↓

Policy Enforcement

↓

Policy Monitoring

↓

↓

Every policy shall have a defined owner, authority, scope, effective period, enforcement mechanism, review frequency, and retirement or evolution condition where applicable.

5.6 Policy Ownership

Every material enterprise policy shall have explicit ownership.

Policy ownership shall define:

policy owner

approving authority

implementation owner

enforcement owner

monitoring owner

assurance owner

review authority

Policy ownership shall remain traceable throughout the policy lifecycle.

No autonomous policy shall remain without a clearly identifiable accountable owner.

5.7 Policy-as-Code

Where technically and operationally appropriate, enterprise policies shall be represented as machine-readable controls.

Policy-as-Code shall enable:

automated policy evaluation

automated enforcement

consistent policy interpretation

continuous compliance validation

automated testing

policy deployment control

governance evidence generation

The policy transformation is:

Human Intent

↓

↓

Formal Policy Rule

↓

Machine-Readable Policy

↓

Policy Engine

↓

Runtime Enforcement

↓

Evidence

Policy-as-Code shall not replace the formal authority of the policy owner.

It shall provide an executable representation of an already authorized governance requirement.

5.8 Policy Decision Points

Autonomous policy enforcement shall identify appropriate decision points.

Decision points may exist:

before execution

during execution

after execution

during exception handling

during system-to-system interaction

during agent-to-agent interaction

during human–AI interaction

The architecture shall apply policy controls according to the risk and consequence associated with the activity.

5.9 Policy Enforcement Modes

Enterprise policies shall be enforceable through several modes.

Advisory Enforcement

The system informs the user or autonomous capability that a policy condition may be violated.

Preventive Enforcement

The system prevents the unauthorized or unsafe action.

Detective Enforcement

The system identifies a violation after or during execution.

Corrective Enforcement

The system initiates an approved corrective action.

Adaptive Enforcement

The system adjusts approved control behavior in response to validated changes in enterprise conditions.

The enforcement progression is:

Advisory

↓

Preventive

↓

Detective

↓

Corrective

↓

Adaptive

The required enforcement mode shall be proportional to risk, consequence, reversibility, and regulatory requirements.

5.10 Policy Conflicts

Autonomous enterprises may encounter conflicting policies.

Policy conflicts shall be identified and resolved through an explicit governance mechanism.

Potential causes include:

overlapping authorities

conflicting business requirements

regulatory changes

outdated policies

inconsistent policy versions

cross-domain dependencies

emergency conditions

conflicting security and operational requirements

Policy conflict handling shall follow:

Conflict Detection

↓

Conflict Classification

↓

Authority Identification

↓

Risk Assessment

↓

Governance Decision

↓

Policy Resolution

↓

Implementation

↓

Evidence

↓

Learning

Autonomous capabilities shall not independently redefine conflicting enterprise policies unless such authority has explicitly been delegated.

5.11 Policy Versioning

Enterprise policies shall be version-controlled.

Policy versions shall maintain:

associated controls

Policy versioning shall enable the enterprise to determine which policy was applicable at the time of an autonomous decision or action.

5.12 Policy Testing

Policies intended for autonomous enforcement shall be tested before production deployment.

Testing shall include, where applicable:

Policy testing shall establish confidence that the policy behaves as intended under both expected and unexpected conditions.

5.13 Policy Observability

Policy execution shall remain observable.

Observability shall provide visibility into:

policy override

policy enforcement

policy failure

Policy observability shall support governance evidence and continuous policy improvement.

5.14 Policy Exceptions

Policy exceptions shall be explicitly governed.

Exceptions shall identify:

authority

scope

Temporary exceptions shall not silently become permanent policy.

↓

Monitoring

↓

Review

The Enterprise Autonomous Policy Engineering Framework shall evaluate:

policy compliance

governance response time

policy lifecycle maturity

automation effectiveness

Performance indicators shall continuously strengthen enterprise policy engineering.

6. Enterprise Autonomous Governance Assurance Framework

6.1 Purpose

The Enterprise Autonomous Governance Assurance Framework establishes the canonical methodology for continuously assessing whether Autonomous Enterprise capabilities remain compliant, controlled, secure, resilient, explainable, accountable, and aligned with enterprise strategy.

Traditional assurance frequently depends upon periodic audits and retrospective reviews.

Autonomous Enterprise assurance must increasingly operate continuously through observability, automated control validation, evidence collection, intelligent analysis, risk assessment, and governance intervention.

Enterprise Architects shall ensure assurance remains independent enough to provide meaningful challenge while sufficiently integrated with enterprise operations to detect emerging issues early.

6.2 Objectives

7. Enterprise Autonomous Governance Risk Management Framework

7.1 Purpose

The Enterprise Autonomous Governance Risk Management Framework establishes the canonical methodology for identifying, assessing, governing, monitoring, mitigating, escalating, and continuously learning from risks arising from increasingly autonomous enterprise capabilities.

Autonomous Enterprise environments introduce risks that may emerge from autonomous decisions, intelligent agents, Artificial Intelligence, automated workflows, interconnected systems, dynamic policies, evolving models, changing information, cyber threats, operational dependencies, and unexpected interactions between enterprise capabilities.

Enterprise Architects shall therefore ensure that autonomous capabilities operate within explicitly defined risk boundaries and that risk management remains integrated with Enterprise Architecture, governance, security, operations, information management, and executive decision-making.

The objective is not to eliminate all risk.

The objective is:

To enable controlled enterprise autonomy within an explicitly defined and continuously monitored risk appetite.

7.2 Objectives

The Enterprise Autonomous Governance Risk Management Framework shall:

establish enterprise-wide autonomous risk management

define autonomous risk boundaries

integrate risk with autonomy decisions

improve emerging risk detection

strengthen risk visibility

improve risk response

strengthen executive risk oversight

enable continuous risk monitoring

improve enterprise resilience

support controlled autonomy

maximize Sustainable Enterprise Value

↓

↓

↓

↓

↓

7.4 Risk Domains

Enterprise Autonomous Governance Risk Management shall govern:

Strategic Risk

Risk arising from autonomous capabilities becoming misaligned with enterprise strategy, strategic priorities, investment objectives, organizational direction, or long-term enterprise development.

Business Risk

Risk arising from autonomous decisions or actions affecting customers, products, services, value streams, business processes, financial performance, or enterprise relationships.

Operational Risk

Risk arising from failures, errors, interruptions, incorrect decisions, process deviations, system dependencies, or unexpected autonomous behavior.

AI Risk

Risk arising from:

model errors

insufficient explainability

Security Risk

Risk arising from:

Compliance Risk

Resilience Risk

The framework establishes governance as an architectural system rather than as a collection of independent committees, procedures, controls, and approval mechanisms.

Enterprise Architects shall ensure that governance architecture provides sufficient control to protect the enterprise while preserving the agility required for intelligent and autonomous operations.

11. Enterprise Autonomous Governance Human Oversight Framework

11.1 Purpose

The Enterprise Autonomous Governance Human Oversight Framework establishes the canonical methodology for ensuring that human authority, judgment, accountability, intervention, and governance remain appropriately integrated into an increasingly autonomous enterprise.

Autonomous Enterprise capabilities may perform analysis, recommendations, decisions, orchestration, execution, monitoring, and optimization.

However, enterprise governance shall retain meaningful human authority wherever decisions involve significant strategic, ethical, financial, regulatory, security, operational, reputational, or irreversible consequences.

Enterprise Architects shall therefore ensure that human oversight is designed according to risk, autonomy level, decision significance, reversibility, regulatory requirements, and enterprise accountability.

The objective is not to require human intervention in every autonomous activity.

The objective is:

To ensure that human authority remains meaningful, proportionate, available, and enforceable wherever enterprise governance requires it.

11.2 Objectives

The Enterprise Autonomous Governance Human Oversight Framework shall:

establish human oversight principles

define human intervention requirements

strengthen executive accountability

establish human override mechanisms

define escalation responsibilities

improve human–AI collaboration

strengthen governance transparency

improve autonomous decision confidence

support responsible autonomy

strengthen enterprise resilience

maximize Sustainable Enterprise Value

11.3 Human Oversight Architecture

The recommended logical architecture consists of:

↓

↓

↓

↓

↓

↓

Execution

↓

Observation

↓

Evidence

↓

Governance Review

↓

Learning

↓

Architecture Evolution

Human oversight shall remain connected to enterprise governance, risk, security, compliance, operational management, and Enterprise Architecture.

11.4 Human Oversight Domains

Human oversight shall govern:

Strategic Oversight

Enterprise strategy, strategic transformation, major investments, enterprise direction, organizational change, and long-term enterprise capability development.

Financial Oversight

Material financial commitments, major expenditures, financial risk, investment decisions, contractual obligations, and significant economic consequences.

Ethical Oversight

Ethical boundaries, responsible AI, human impact, fairness, organizational values, stakeholder interests, and socially significant decisions.

Regulatory Oversight

Material regulatory obligations, legal requirements, compliance decisions, regulated activities, and significant regulatory risk.

Security Oversight

Critical cybersecurity decisions, security exceptions, major incidents, privileged access, cyber response, and security risk acceptance.

Operational Oversight

Critical service decisions, operational continuity, major incidents, resilience decisions, and significant operational changes.

Architecture Oversight

Major architecture decisions, significant architectural exceptions, technology direction, enterprise transformation, and material architectural risk.

Autonomous Capability Oversight

Autonomy levels, delegated authority, agent behavior, AI model changes, capability boundaries, escalation conditions, and capability suspension.

11.5 Human Oversight Levels

EA-IMETA76 establishes five human oversight levels.

Level 1 – Direct Human Control

The human performs the decision and execution.

AI and automation provide supporting information only.

Level 2 – Human Approval

The autonomous capability prepares the decision or action.

Human approval is required before execution.

Level 3 – Human Supervision

The autonomous capability executes approved activities.

Humans monitor performance and intervene when predefined conditions are triggered.

Level 4 – Human Governance

The autonomous capability operates independently within approved boundaries.

Humans govern policy, authority, risk, performance, exceptions, and capability evolution.

Level 5 – Human Strategic Direction

The autonomous enterprise operates with high operational autonomy while humans retain responsibility for:

enterprise purpose

strategic direction

governance principles

risk appetite

ethical boundaries

major enterprise decisions

organizational accountability

The appropriate level shall be determined according to risk and enterprise consequence.

11.6 Human Intervention Conditions

Human intervention shall be required when:

autonomous authority is exceeded

risk thresholds are exceeded

decision confidence is insufficient

policy conflicts exist

material uncertainty emerges

ethical concerns arise

regulatory requirements require human judgment

financial consequences exceed approved thresholds

security conditions materially change

operational resilience is threatened

autonomous behavior becomes abnormal

critical dependencies fail

stakeholders require human involvement

Intervention conditions shall be explicitly defined before autonomous deployment.

11.7 Human Override

The enterprise shall maintain effective mechanisms for overriding autonomous decisions and actions.

Override mechanisms may include:

decision override

transaction cancellation

workflow interruption

agent suspension

authority revocation

service isolation

emergency shutdown

policy enforcement

capability restriction

Override mechanisms shall be:

authorized

protected

observable

tested

auditable

recoverable where appropriate

An override capability that exists only theoretically shall not be considered an effective governance control.

11.8 Escalation Architecture

Human escalation shall follow a defined authority path.

↓

↓

Capability Owner

↓

Governance Authority

↓

Executive Authority

↓

Enterprise Leadership

Escalation shall be directed to the lowest appropriate authority capable of resolving the condition.

Critical events shall bypass normal escalation paths when predefined emergency conditions require immediate executive or operational intervention.

11.9 Human Oversight Evidence

intervention

override

escalation

authority

decision

rationale

outcome

exception

policy application

Evidence shall support:

accountability

audit

compliance

governance review

continuous learning

response time

decision quality

human–AI collaboration quality

governance confidence

stakeholder confidence

autonomy maturity

Sustainable Enterprise Value realization

Performance indicators shall continuously strengthen human oversight maturity.

12. Enterprise Autonomous Governance Lifecycle Framework

12.1 Purpose

The Enterprise Autonomous Governance Lifecycle Framework establishes the canonical lifecycle through which autonomous governance capabilities are conceived, designed, authorized, implemented, operated, assured, improved, and ultimately retired or transformed.

The lifecycle ensures that governance remains active throughout the complete existence of an autonomous capability rather than being concentrated only during initial design or periodic review.

Enterprise Architects shall ensure each autonomous capability has a defined governance lifecycle covering strategy, design, authorization, deployment, operation, monitoring, assurance, evolution, suspension, and retirement.

12.2 Objectives

establish a complete governance lifecycle

12.5 Governance Lifecycle Gates

Gate 8 – Retirement Approval

Confirms controlled suspension or retirement.

regulatory impact

13. Enterprise Autonomous Governance Maturity Framework

13.1 Purpose

The Enterprise Autonomous Governance Maturity Framework establishes the canonical methodology for assessing the maturity, readiness, effectiveness, resilience, and evolutionary capability of governance within an Autonomous Enterprise.

Autonomous governance maturity shall not be measured solely by the amount of governance automation implemented.

A mature governance model must demonstrate that the enterprise can:

define authority;

control autonomous capabilities;

enforce policy;

observe execution;

manage risk;

provide meaningful human oversight;

generate evidence;

respond to exceptions;

learn from outcomes;

evolve governance continuously.

Enterprise Architects shall therefore assess governance maturity across organizational, architectural, technological, operational, human, AI, agent, information, security, risk, and assurance dimensions.

The objective is to establish a measurable path from conventional governance toward continuously adaptive autonomous governance.

13.2 Objectives

The Enterprise Autonomous Governance Maturity Framework shall:

establish a common governance maturity model

assess autonomous governance readiness

identify governance capability gaps

define governance improvement priorities

support autonomous capability authorization

strengthen executive governance confidence

align governance maturity with autonomy maturity

establish measurable governance evolution

support continuous assurance

maximize Sustainable Enterprise Value

13.3 Governance Maturity Architecture

The recommended logical architecture consists of:

Governance Baseline

↓

Capability Assessment

↓

Maturity Assessment

↓

Gap Analysis

↓

Governance Improvement

↓

Autonomy Readiness

↓

Controlled Implementation

↓

Performance Measurement

↓

Continuous Learning

↓

Governance Evolution

Governance maturity shall be assessed before materially increasing the degree of enterprise autonomy.

13.4 Governance Maturity Levels

EA-IMETA76 establishes the following governance maturity levels.

Level 0 – Unstructured Governance

Governance is primarily informal, reactive, and dependent upon individual knowledge.

Characteristics include:

undocumented authority;

inconsistent policies;

limited observability;

reactive risk management;

limited evidence;

manual governance intervention.

Autonomous operation shall remain highly restricted.

Level 1 – Defined Governance

Basic governance structures and policies have been established.

Characteristics include:

documented policies;

identified owners;

basic decision rights;

defined responsibilities;

basic risk management;

initial governance reporting.

Governance remains primarily human-driven.

Level 2 – Managed Governance

Governance processes are standardized and measured.

Characteristics include:

defined governance lifecycle;

structured authority;

policy management;

governance metrics;

formal exception management;

regular assurance.

Selected autonomous capabilities may operate within clearly defined boundaries.

Level 3 – Integrated Governance

Governance is integrated across Enterprise Architecture, business, information, technology, security, risk, and operations.

Characteristics include:

integrated governance architecture;

shared governance information;

cross-domain controls;

continuous monitoring;

integrated risk management;

governance evidence.

Autonomous operating capabilities may be deployed at scale within controlled domains.

Level 4 – Intelligent Governance

Governance becomes intelligence-enabled.

Characteristics include:

predictive risk analysis;

governance intelligence;

automated policy evaluation;

AI-assisted assurance;

intelligent anomaly detection;

decision support;

continuous control validation.

Governance becomes increasingly proactive.

Level 5 – Autonomous Governance

Governance capabilities can autonomously monitor, evaluate, control, escalate, and optimize approved governance activities within defined authority.

Characteristics include:

Policy-as-Code;

autonomous control execution;

intelligent governance orchestration;

continuous assurance;

autonomous exception detection;

dynamic risk monitoring;

automated evidence generation.

Human governance remains the source of enterprise purpose, policy, authority, and accountability.

Level 6 – Adaptive Autonomous Governance

Governance continuously adapts to validated changes in:

enterprise strategy;

risk;

regulation;

technology;

operating conditions;

AI capabilities;

agent capabilities;

enterprise performance.

The governance architecture can recommend and, where authorized, implement bounded improvements while maintaining traceability and accountability.

Level 7 – Continuously Evolving Governance

Governance operates as a continuously learning enterprise capability.

The architecture continuously connects:

Intent → Policy → Authority → Control → Execution → Evidence → Assurance → Learning → Evolution

Governance evolution remains bounded by enterprise purpose, strategic authority, ethical principles, regulatory requirements, and approved governance constraints.

13.5 Maturity Assessment Domains

Governance maturity shall be assessed across:

Strategy

Alignment between governance and enterprise purpose.

Organization

Governance roles, responsibilities, ownership, and accountability.

Architecture

Governance integration with Enterprise Architecture.

Policy

Policy quality, enforceability, lifecycle management, and Policy-as-Code maturity.

Authority

Decision rights, delegation, autonomy boundaries, and revocation.

Risk

Risk identification, assessment, monitoring, and response.

Security

Identity, Zero Trust, cybersecurity, resilience, and security governance.

AI

AI governance, model governance, explainability, and AI assurance.

Agents

Agent identity, authority, behavior, tool access, and lifecycle governance.

Operations

Operational controls, observability, exception management, and intervention.

Assurance

Evidence, auditability, compliance, and continuous control validation.

Intelligence

Predictive governance, governance analytics, and decision support.

Learning

Continuous improvement, feedback, and governance evolution.

13.6 Governance Readiness for Autonomy

The enterprise shall not increase autonomy solely because the underlying technology is available.

Autonomy readiness shall consider:

governance maturity;

risk maturity;

observability;

policy maturity;

authority maturity;

human oversight;

security maturity;

resilience;

evidence quality;

intervention capability.

The relationship shall be:

Governance Maturity

+

Risk Maturity

+

Operational Maturity

+

Technology Maturity

+

Human Oversight

=

Autonomy Readiness

13.7 Governance Maturity Assessment

Assessment shall evaluate:

current maturity;

target maturity;

maturity gaps;

critical weaknesses;

improvement opportunities;

autonomy constraints;

required investments;

governance risks.

The assessment shall produce an actionable governance improvement roadmap.

13.8 Governance Improvement Lifecycle

Governance maturity improvement shall progress through:

Assess

↓

Identify Gaps

↓

Prioritize

↓

Design Improvement

↓

Approve

↓

Implement

↓

Measure

↓

Validate

↓

Learn

↓

Evolve

Improvement shall be governed as an enterprise transformation activity.

13.9 Governance Maturity Performance

The Enterprise Autonomous Governance Maturity Framework shall evaluate:

governance maturity

autonomy readiness

policy maturity

authority maturity

risk maturity

assurance maturity

observability maturity

human oversight maturity

AI governance maturity

agent governance maturity

governance intelligence maturity

Sustainable Enterprise Value realization

Performance indicators shall continuously strengthen governance maturity.

14. Enterprise Autonomous Governance Reference Model

14.1 Purpose

The Enterprise Autonomous Governance Reference Model establishes the consolidated reference architecture for the governance of the Autonomous Enterprise.

It brings together the governance structures, authority mechanisms, policies, controls, decision models, risk mechanisms, human oversight, assurance capabilities, governance intelligence, lifecycle management, and maturity mechanisms established throughout EA-IMETA76 Part 1.

The model provides a single coherent reference for understanding:

14.2 Reference Model Architecture

Each layer shall remain connected to the layers above and below it.

14.3 Reference Model Domains

The EA-IMETA76 Autonomous Governance Reference Model shall contain the following domains.

Domain 1 – Enterprise Purpose

Defines why the enterprise exists and the outcomes it seeks to achieve.

Domain 2 – Strategic Governance

Defines enterprise direction, strategic objectives, risk appetite, and executive authority.

Domain 3 – Architecture Governance

Defines architectural principles, target architecture, standards, decisions, and architectural constraints.

Domain 4 – Policy Governance

Defines enterprise policies, rules, requirements, standards, and enforceable controls.

Domain 5 – Authority Governance

Defines decision rights, delegated authority, autonomy boundaries, ownership, accountability, and revocation.

Domain 6 – Decision Governance

Defines how human, AI-assisted, AI-recommended, autonomous, and automated decisions are governed.

Domain 7 – Autonomous Capability Governance

Defines the lifecycle, behavior, authority, tools, information access, and operating conditions of autonomous capabilities.

Domain 8 – Operational Governance

Defines how autonomous capabilities operate within enterprise processes, services, workflows, and operating models.

Domain 9 – Risk and Security Governance

Defines risk boundaries, security controls, Zero Trust, cyber resilience, and risk response.

Domain 10 – Human Oversight

Defines human intervention, approval, override, escalation, suspension, and strategic direction.

Domain 11 – Assurance

Defines compliance, control validation, auditability, evidence, independent review, and continuous assurance.

Domain 12 – Governance Intelligence

Defines governance analytics, predictive insight, decision support, anomaly detection, and governance intelligence.

Domain 13 – Governance Learning

Defines feedback, lessons learned, performance evaluation, and governance improvement.

Domain 14 – Governance Evolution

Defines how governance architecture, policies, authorities, controls, operating models, and autonomous capabilities evolve.

14.4 Integrated Governance Control Loop

The complete EA-IMETA76 governance control loop is:

This closed-loop architecture establishes governance as a continuously operating enterprise capability.

14.5 Governance Traceability

The reference model shall support end-to-end traceability.

The enterprise shall be able to trace:

Purpose → Strategy → Policy → Authority → Capability → Decision → Action → Outcome → Evidence → Assurance → Learning

This traceability shall support:

accountability;

auditability;

compliance;

14.6 Governance Reference Model Principles

The consolidated reference model shall remain:

Instead:

14.7 EA-IMETA76 Part 1 Governance Synthesis

The first part of EA-IMETA76 establishes a complete governance foundation for the Autonomous Enterprise.

The resulting governance architecture connects:

14.8 Part 1 Governance Operating Principle

The central operating principle of EA-IMETA76 Part 1 is:

Enterprise autonomy shall be delegated, bounded, observable, evidence-based, risk-proportional, human-accountable, and continuously governed.

This principle establishes the foundation for the remaining parts of EA-IMETA76.

The governance model shall therefore evolve from:

Governance of Autonomous Systems

toward:

Autonomous Governance of the Enterprise

while preserving human authority over:

enterprise purpose;

strategic direction;

governance principles;

ethical boundaries;

risk appetite;

major enterprise decisions;

accountability.

intelligence-enabled

evidence-driven

resilient

measurable

continuously evolving

These implementation characteristics establish the consolidated governance foundation of the Autonomous Enterprise, enabling Enterprise Architects to assess governance maturity, determine autonomy readiness, establish integrated governance architecture, maintain explicit authority, provide meaningful human oversight, continuously assure autonomous operations, and evolve governance as enterprise conditions change.

Part 1 Conclusion

EA-IMETA76 Part 1 establishes the foundational Enterprise Autonomous Governance & Operating Model.

The complete governance cycle is:

Purpose → Strategy → Policy → Authority → Autonomy → Decision → Execution → Observation → Evidence → Assurance → Intervention → Learning → Evolution

The central architectural principle is:

Autonomy shall never exist outside governance, and governance shall continuously evolve to remain capable of governing autonomy.

Part 1 therefore establishes the governance foundation upon which the subsequent EA-IMETA76 parts shall build the broader Autonomous Enterprise Governance & Operating Model.

The resulting enterprise governance capability is intended to provide:

controlled autonomy;

explicit authority;

continuous observability;

policy-driven execution;

measurable risk;

meaningful human oversight;

auditable decisions;

continuous assurance;

governance intelligence;

lifecycle control;

Sustainable Enterprise Value.
